fact_sheet.business_description: The Company sells branded beverage concentrates through a global bottling and distribution system [D01]. It focuses on the beverage franchise, leveraging strong consumer recognition and repeat demand for its flagship products [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Branded beverage concentrates sold to bottlers and retailers who manage production, packaging, and distribution to consumers [D01, D06].
Consumer loyalty is evidenced by repeat demand and recognition of the flagship product [D01, D06].
economics: Concentrate model separates the brand from the capital-intensive bottling business [D01, D06].
Return on average equity from continuing operations was 27.2% in 1987 and 28.8% in 1986 [D02].
Currency strengthening and international growth are key drivers, with international markets accounting for ~65% of volume and ~77% of operating income [D06].
earnings_record: Earnings reflect cyclicality and non-operating restructuring charges of $180m in 1986 and $36m in 1987 [D02, D03].
competitive_position: Global soft-drink share of more than 44% (excluding Soviet Union/China) [D06].
Fountain business holds a greater than two-to-one lead over its nearest rival [D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Cash plus marketable securities were $1.468bn at year-end 1987 [D02].
The model relies on bottlers to supply physical capital, though the producer remains exposed to currency and regulation risks [D01, D06].
management_and_capital_allocation: CEO tenure began in 1981, focusing on the beverage franchise and financial discipline [D01].
Strategy emphasizes expansion abroad and efficient capital allocation [D03].
price_and_valuation: Earnings yield of 6.37% (vs 8.87% for 10-year Treasury as of Sept 30, 1988) [D04].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Dilution from capital-heavy bottling investments or unrelated activities [D05].
Fragility of competitive advantages against aggressive competitors [D05].
recent_events: Second-quarter 1988 net income rose 13.8% to $303m, aided by European/Pacific sales [D03].
berkshire_context: The Company is not an existing position mentioned in the fund context [D08].
Existing major holdings include Capital Cities/ABC, GEICO, and Washington Post [D08].
document_conflicts: The 1986 return on equity is cited as 28.8% in [D02], correcting an erroneous 23.8% found in secondary transcriptions [D02].
missing_data: Current September 30, 1988 stock price, market capitalization, and trailing earnings multiple.
Up-to-date maintenance capital expenditure figures for owner earnings bridge.

understandable.evidence: The company maintains a clear, long-standing focus on its global beverage franchise and brand recognition [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: A global soft-drink share exceeding 44% and a greater than two-to-one lead in the fountain business demonstrate significant competitive advantages [D06].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: The company has shown strong consistent earnings growth, despite minor, non-recurring restructuring charges [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: Return on average equity has been consistently strong, reaching 27.2% in 1987 [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The concentrate business model successfully separates the brand from the capital-intensive bottling operations [D01].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: Management has focused on the core beverage franchise and disciplined financial allocation since 1981 [D01, D03].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: As a major global entity, the business is of a scale that can significantly impact Berkshire's portfolio [D06].

price_screen.evidence: The 1987 earnings yield of 6.37% is well below our 10% threshold and lower than the 10-year Treasury yield of 8.87% [D04].

conflicts_resolved: 28.8% ROE for 1986 in [D02] used over erroneous 23.8% transcription per the fact sheet [D02].
gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: a wonderful global beverage franchise with a massive moat and high returns on capital

gate2.why_available: The market is fixated on short-term factors like potential brand overvaluation and the risk of dilution from bottling investments, leading to a valuation that ignores the underlying durability of the franchise [D05]. We view these concerns as transient and believe the market under-estimates the compounding power of the global beverage brand and its significant international growth runway [D01, D06]. The value will manifest as earnings grow and the market eventually recognizes the consistency and pricing power of this wonderful business [D02, D03].
evidence: Global soft-drink share exceeding 44% with a strong international presence [D06].
High return on average equity, reaching 27.2% in 1987 [D02].
Second-quarter 1988 net income growth of 13.8%, demonstrating continued momentum [D03].
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market fears that the competitive advantages are fragile, international growth will disappoint, and that capital-intensive bottling investments will dilute returns [D05].
what_must_be_true: The brand's consumer loyalty and pricing power remain intact despite competitive pressures.
Management continues to focus on disciplined capital allocation rather than excessive diversification.
International markets continue to act as a significant driver of volume and earnings growth.
The concentrate business model maintains its capital-light advantage.

intrinsic_value_range.low: Under valuation as a wonderful business [D01, D06]

gate3.price_vs_value: Price reflects temporary market fixation on bottling investment dilution; provides opportunity for a wonderful business [D05]
gate3.alternatives: 10-year Treasury yields 8.87% [D04]; Coca-Cola offers superior long-term compounding of owner earnings compared to fixed-income alternatives [D01, D06]
gate3.downside_case: If growth stalls or competitive position weakens, the downside is limited by the brand's global scale and entrenched distribution system [D06]
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capex assumed to be nominal relative to reported depreciation [D01]
Assumed stable share count for EPS approximation [D02]

gate4.role_description: We are a permanent passive holder. We do not seek to control or manage, but rather to participate in the long-term earnings power and compounding of a wonderful business [D01]. We rely on management's ability to allocate capital and grow the franchise [D03].
value_realisation_path: Earnings growth driven by international expansion and pricing power [D06]
Market recognition of the business's consistent performance over the long term [D02]
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: For marketable securities in the 1980-1999 era, our edge is patience and permanent capital; we seek wonderful consumer franchises at fair prices and hold them for the long term [D01, D06].

kill_criteria: pricing power lost to private label or significant shift in consumer preference
management acquires outside its competence or over-leverages to chase growth
regulator or geopolitical instability disrupts international distribution or concentrate margins
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Must maintain adequate liquidity for insurance operations; must navigate potential antitrust scrutiny if ownership exceeds 10% thresholds [D01, D06].
gate5.opportunity_cost: 10-year Treasury yields 8.87%, which is higher than the current earnings yield [D04], but Coca-Cola offers superior long-term compounding of owner earnings [D01, D06].
gate5.decider_reason: This is a quintessential consumer franchise with a durable moat that fits squarely within my circle of competence and allows for a significant long-term position.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is that the market's concern regarding the dilution of returns from capital-intensive bottling investments proves to be a permanent impairment of owner earnings rather than a transient strategic transition.

valuation.downside_case: Limited by the brand's global scale and entrenched distribution system

drivers.driver: A global soft-drink share exceeding 44% provides an enduring moat and exceptional pricing power [D06].
The concentrate business model separates the brand from capital-intensive bottling, resulting in highly attractive returns on equity [D01, D02].
Management has demonstrated disciplined capital allocation and a singular focus on the core beverage franchise since 1981 [D01, D03].
The market's temporary fixation on bottling investments and dilution concerns offers us an entry point into a wonderful business at a fair price [D05].

kill_criteria: pricing power lost to private label or significant shift in consumer preference
management acquires outside its competence or over-leverages to chase growth
regulator or geopolitical instability disrupts international distribution or concentrate margins
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A permanent degradation in the brand's consumer loyalty or the company's ability to maintain its capital-light concentrate business model.
final.memo:
Coca-Cola is a business we have long admired, operating a global beverage franchise that we understand perfectly [D01]. It sells branded concentrates to a vast network of bottlers, maintaining a direct and powerful connection with consumers that is evidenced by a global soft-drink share exceeding 44% [D01, D06].

This is a wonderful business with a durable moat, requiring very little of its own capital to grow [D01]. The economics are exceptional, as demonstrated by a 27.2% return on average equity in 1987, and the company benefits from a greater than two-to-one lead in the fountain business [D02, D06].

Since 1981, management has focused exclusively on the core franchise and has been remarkably disciplined in its capital allocation [D01]. We have full confidence in their ability to continue expanding this franchise globally, where international markets already drive roughly 77% of operating income [D03, D06].

The market currently frets about the potential for dilution from bottling investments and brand valuation concerns [D05]. We view these as transient issues that ignore the immense compounding power of the business, which continues to deliver strong income growth, such as the 13.8% increase in net income during the second quarter of 1988 [D03, D05].

While the initial earnings yield is lower than the 10-year Treasury, the long-term compounding of owner earnings makes this a superior alternative [D04, D06]. We believe the intrinsic value will grow substantially over time, providing us with a margin of safety that fixed-income investments simply cannot match [D01, D06].

We intend to build a position toward 20% of our equity portfolio, as the business's scale and quality are a perfect fit for Berkshire [D05, D06]. We are willing to hold this indefinitely, provided the brand loyalty remains intact and the company avoids over-leveraging or diversifying into inferior businesses [D01, D05].
